intro:
This track is about batch jobs: programs that read a big, fixed pile of data in one run and work out an answer from all of it, such as each shop's takings for the night. Lessons start from scenes everyone knows: a jar of coins counted on New Year's Eve, a tally of ballots that outgrows its sheet, a library counting books in forty branches, a café menu changed one price card at a time, and a night shift whose report counts one day twice. Then they open up the tools that do this work at scale, with real runs on your laptop.

By the end, you can:

- say what a job will cost before it runs: the bytes it reads after skipping days and columns, and whether one machine can do it in time;
- count with a hash map or a sort on one machine, and follow the same work through MapReduce and Spark: tasks, stages, the shuffle that moves rows between machines, and the joins that ride on it;
- keep payments as a star of tables that remembers history, stored as Parquet files in an Apache Iceberg table that changes in one step, takes corrections and stays fast;
- run the nightly jobs in order, safe to retry and to rerun for past days;
- hand their output to analysts, to training data that never sees the future, and to a live app all at once;
- pick DuckDB, Spark, Trino or a streaming engine by the numbers.

The fifteen lessons:

1. Why big data systems exist, and when you don't need one
2. Batch on one machine: pipes, sorting and hashing
3. HDFS and MapReduce: the ideas that survived
4. Hive: SQL on files, partitions and the metastore
5. Columnar files: Parquet internals and pushdown
6. The Spark execution model
7. The shuffle, partitioning and joins
8. The optimizer, AQE, skew and caching
9. Spark 4 for JVM engineers: Connect, ANSI and VARIANT
10. Warehouses and dimensional models: OLAP and star schemas
11. Lakehouse tables with Apache Iceberg
12. Row-level changes, compaction and catalogs
13. Orchestrating batch work: DAGs, retries and backfills
14. What batch output is for: ETL, ML features and serving data
15. Choosing an engine: DuckDB, Spark, Trino and friends

You need to read a little code, in Kotlin or Java. You don't need any background in big data: every term is explained the first time it appears in a lesson. Earlier tracks help, and lessons name them when they lean on them: column storage from Storage engines and query execution, Kafka from Messaging and logs, and Spark's streaming side from Stream processing.

The labs are Kotlin with JUnit tests, one package per lesson (`sfz.batch.l01` to `sfz.batch.l15`). Most live in `labs/bigdata`. It runs Spark 4.1.4 (the newest line that both Iceberg 1.12 and Delta Lake 4.4 support), Iceberg and DuckDB inside the test program itself, on a JDK 21 that Gradle fetches for you, so there's no cluster, Hadoop or Docker to set up. Lessons 2, 13 and 14 are plain Kotlin simulations in `labs/sim` that run in a second. From the `labs` folder, run `./gradlew :bigdata:test --tests 'sfz.batch.lNN.*'` (or `:sim:` for lessons 2, 13 and 14) until it passes, and `./gradlew :bigdata:demo -Pmain=...` for the Try it demos. Spark tests share one local session, so the first test of a run pays a few seconds to start. Timings in the lessons were measured on a busy laptop: trust the ratios and the shapes, not the milliseconds.
cheatsheet:
## The cost of a scan (lessons 1, 2 and 15)

A batch job's time is mostly reading: `time = bytes read / speed of the slowest stage` (the disk, the network, or the processor decoding). 1 TB at 500 MB/s is 2,000 s. There are two levers: more readers (split the work over machines) and fewer bytes (fewer columns, compression, skipping files that can't match). Pull "fewer bytes" first.

| Step | Example: 4 TB, 3 years, 60 columns |
|---|---|
| Partitions read (the days the filter keeps) | 30 of 1,095 days: 110 GB |
| Columns read | 4 of 60: 7.3 GB |
| One machine's speed | the slower of (cores x decode speed) and storage speed: about 3 GB/s on a laptop, 1.5 GB/s on a cloud machine reading S3 |
| People sharing it | time x the queries running at once |
| Working set (what must sit in memory at once) | a join's hash table, or one total per group: it must fit in memory |

On one machine, a hash map counts in one pass while the different keys fit in memory. When they don't, an external merge sort writes sorted runs the size of its buffer M and merges them F at a time: about N / M runs and ceil(log_F(runs)) passes. `sort | uniq -c` is already a map, a shuffle and a reduce.

## Files over many machines, and MapReduce (lessons 3 and 4)

- HDFS, Hadoop's file system, cuts files into 128 MB blocks, keeps 3 copies of each, and keeps the map of blocks on one NameNode. MapReduce runs map, sends each pair to reducer `hash(key) mod R` through local disk (the shuffle), sorts, then reduces. A combiner adds up early, on the map side, only for work where grouping and order don't change the answer; for an average, carry `(sum, count)`.
- Object stores such as S3 replaced HDFS: they're cheap, they grow as needed, and there's no NameNode. They aren't file systems: there's no rename, a LIST returns 1,000 keys per call, and 100 to 200 ms pass before the first byte. Since 2020, S3 is strongly consistent (a read sees the last write). Since 2024, it has conditional writes: `If-None-Match: *` creates a file only if it's absent, and `If-Match` replaces it only if its ETag, a fingerprint of the contents, still matches.
- Hive: a table is a folder plus a description in the metastore. Partitions are folders such as `dt=2026-11-07/`, skipped only when the query filters on the partition column. Writes aren't all or nothing, and each small file costs one more open.

## Parquet (lesson 5)

A Parquet file holds row groups (slices of rows), each with one column chunk per column, split into pages. Then comes a footer with offsets and min, max and null counts, which a reader reads first. Each column is encoded (dictionary, run-length, delta), then compressed with Snappy or Zstd. Min and max let a reader skip whole row groups, but only when the rows are sorted or grouped by the filter column.

## Spark (lessons 6 to 9)

| Idea | Rule |
|---|---|
| A lazy plan | transformations (`where`, `groupBy`, `join`) only build a plan; actions (`count`, `collect`, `write`) run it, every time again |
| Stages | split at each `Exchange` (a shuffle); one task per partition; extra tasks wait and run in waves |
| Failure | a task is retried up to 4 times from its lineage; lost shuffle files rerun the map tasks that wrote them |
| Shuffle | M x R blocks; `spark.sql.shuffle.partitions` is 200 by default: set it high and let AQE merge |
| Joins | a broadcast hash join copies the small table to every executor, under 10 MB or with `broadcast()`; otherwise a sort-merge join shuffles both sides |
| AQE (planning again while the query runs) | at each shuffle: merges small partitions, switches to a broadcast, splits skewed partitions (over 5x the median and 256 MB) |
| Skew (one key with far more rows) | one slow task: AQE's skew join or salting the key; speculation doesn't help |
| `cache()` | pays only when the result is reused; `unpersist()` after |
| Spark 4 | Connect: a thin client sends plans over gRPC (port 15002). ANSI mode is on: bad casts fail, so use `try_cast`. VARIANT: JSON read once. The labs pin 4.1.4, because Iceberg 1.12 stops at 4.1 |

Read plans with `explain("formatted")`, and look for `Exchange hashpartitioning`, `BroadcastExchange`, `SortMergeJoin`, `AQEShuffleRead` and `InMemoryTableScan`.

## Warehouses and star schemas (lesson 10)

Declare the grain, what one row stands for. Then build a fact table (events: keys and numbers to add up) with dimension tables around it (who, what, where, when). A star keeps each dimension flat, one join away. A snowflake splits dimensions into more tables and more joins. One big table copies every description onto every fact: cheap to store in a column store, costly to correct.

| When a shop changes (slowly changing dimension) | What the change does |
|---|---|
| Type 0 | never changes |
| Type 1 | overwrite: history is rewritten (fine for corrections) |
| Type 2 | close the version (`valid_to`, `is_current = false`) and insert a new one with a new surrogate key; each fact keeps the key that was valid on its day |
| Type 3 | one previous value, in its own column |
| Types 6 and 7 | the current value on every version, or a lasting key on the fact, for reports "as things are now" |

Engines copy small dimensions to every machine, and turn the keys that survive the dimension filters into a filter on the fact table's read at run time (DuckDB's dynamic filters, Spark's dynamic partition pruning, Snowflake's runtime pruning). In Redshift, KEY distribution puts rows with the same join key on the same machine, ALL copies a table to every machine, and AUTO decides.

## Table formats and catalogs (lessons 11 and 12)

| Layer | Example | What it holds |
|---|---|---|
| File format | Parquet | one file's rows, by column, with statistics |
| Table format | Iceberg 1.12, Delta 4.4, Hudi 1.2, DuckLake 1.1 | which files make each version, the schemas, partition specs and snapshots |
| Catalog | a Hadoop folder, JDBC, Hive Metastore, REST (Polaris, Unity Catalog) | each table's pointer, and the compare-and-swap that commits |

Iceberg's tree: a pointer, `vN.metadata.json`, one manifest list per snapshot, manifests with statistics for each file, then the Parquet files. A commit writes new files, then swaps the pointer only if it still names the version the writer started from; the loser retries. `VERSION AS OF` reads the past until its snapshot expires. Hidden partitioning: `PARTITIONED BY (days(created_at))`.

| Changing rows | Writes | Reads |
|---|---|---|
| copy-on-write (the default) | rewrites every file that holds a changed row | plain files |
| merge-on-read, format v2 | the new rows + position delete files (file, row) | merge in the deletes |
| merge-on-read, format v3 | the new rows + one deletion vector per data file | one bitmap per file |

Upkeep, in this order: `rewrite_data_files` (compaction, in a `replace` snapshot), `expire_snapshots` (ends time travel to them), `remove_orphan_files` (leftovers older than 3 days by default; it refuses anything under 24 hours).

## Orchestration (lesson 13)

Three layers schedule. The workflow orchestrator (Airflow 3, Dagster, Prefect) decides when each job runs, in what order and for which logical date, the day of data a run is for. The engine (Spark's driver) runs a job's tasks and retries them. The resource manager (Kubernetes, YARN) decides which machine runs each program.

A task is safe to retry or backfill (rerun for past days) when it reads its logical date's partition, never `now()` or "the latest", and replaces that date's output in one step: overwrite the partition, delete and insert inside one transaction, or `MERGE`. Outside effects, such as emails, go in their own task with a record of what was done. Speculation (`spark.speculation`, off by default) rescues slow machines, not skew.

`airflow backfill create --dag-id d --from-date ... --to-date ... --reprocess-behavior none|failed|completed --max-active-runs N --run-backwards`. Time = ceil(days / N) waves x the run time. Backfill tasks don't wait behind tonight's runs, so cap N.

## Batch output (lesson 14)

- ELT: load the raw data, then reshape it inside the warehouse with SQL. dbt models are `SELECT`s, run in the order their `ref()` links give.
- Training data: a point-in-time join. For a label at time t, take the newest feature row whose event time <= t and write time <= t, within a TTL. A join to today's features leaks the future.
- Serving: never write row by row into the live database. Publish through Kafka with a "run complete" marker, or build files offline (RocksDB's `SstFileWriter` + `IngestExternalFile`) and switch versions by replacing one pointer in one step (a rename over `CURRENT`). Rollback = publish the previous version again.

## Engines (lesson 15)

| Engine | Use it for |
|---|---|
| DuckDB 2.0 | anything one machine reads in time: one-off questions, reports, tests; reads Parquet and Iceberg where they lie |
| Polars 2.1, pandas 3.1 | DataFrames on one machine: Polars plans first and can spill to disk, pandas runs each step at once, in memory |
| Spark | long batch jobs, backfills, big joins and shuffles, Structured Streaming |
| Trino 484 | SQL that answers in seconds for many people, over the lake and other sources (needs Java 25) |
| ClickHouse | answers in well under a second on fresh events, from its own storage |
| Flink | streaming as the product: a reaction to each event, very large state |
recap: A scan costs the bytes it reads, divided by the speed of the slowest stage. Read fewer bytes (fewer columns, compression, skipped days and blocks) before adding machines, and size every job by the bytes it reads after skipping, not by the size of the table.

One machine goes far: a hash map while the keys fit in memory, an external merge sort when they don't. A cluster earns its overhead only when the data, the deadline or the working set outgrows one machine.

MapReduce's ideas survived: blocks read in parallel, map then shuffle by key then reduce, rerunning tasks that always give the same answer, and output that appears in one step. Object stores replaced HDFS, and their conditional writes (since 2024) give a commit the compare-and-swap it needs.

Spark builds a lazy plan, its optimizer rewrites it, and each shuffle splits a job into stages. Most tuning is about the shuffle: how many partitions, broadcast or sort-merge joins, and hot keys, which AQE or salting fix and speculation doesn't.
Spark 4 runs thin clients over Connect, stops loudly on bad data in ANSI mode and stores JSON as VARIANT. This track pins 4.1, the newest line that Iceberg 1.12 and Delta 4.4 both support.

A warehouse keeps events as a fact table at a declared grain, with flat dimensions around it. It keeps changing descriptions as type 2 versions with surrogate keys, and runs star queries by copying dimensions to every machine and pushing their keys into the fact table's read.

A lakehouse table is Parquet files that never change, plus a tree of metadata committed by one compare-and-swap in a catalog. That gives one-step commits, snapshots, reading the past, safe schema and partition changes, and row corrections that need compaction and snapshot expiry.

Every layer retries, so batch tasks must be safe to run twice: read the logical date's partition and replace its output in one step. Then retries and backfills are safe; cap backfills so the nightly runs keep running.
Batch output feeds analysts (ELT with dbt), models (point-in-time training data that never sees the future) and live apps (stores built offline and switched by one pointer, never written row by row).

With one copy of the data in an open table format, each piece of work picks its engine by the numbers: DuckDB or Polars when one machine is enough, Trino for shared SQL in seconds, Spark for heavy batch, a streaming engine for work that never ends. The limit: the numbers count bytes and seconds, not money or the work of running each engine.

quiz.q: A 5 TB payments table holds 2 years of daily partitions and 50 columns of similar size. An analyst's query reads 5 columns of the last 10 days. Which estimate should decide the engine?
options: 5 TB, the size of the table
About 68 GB, the last 10 days
About 6.8 GB: 10 of 730 days and 5 of 50 columns, a few seconds on one machine
The number of rows, because engines process rows
quiz.why: 5 TB x 10 / 730 is 68 GB for the days, and x 5 / 50 is 6.8 GB for the columns. At 2 to 3 GB/s, that's a few seconds on one machine. 68 GB forgets that Parquet reads only the columns a query uses; 5 TB forgets skipping altogether.

quiz.q: A Kotlin job counts payments per card with a `HashMap<String, Long>`. With 200 million different cards, it dies with OutOfMemoryError. What keeps it on one machine?
options: Switch to a `TreeMap`
An external merge sort: sort runs that fit in memory, write them to disk, merge them, then count equal keys that sit next to each other
Nothing: it needs a cluster
Count in parallel threads with the same map
quiz.why: The hash map's memory grows with the number of different keys, about 100 bytes plus the key each on the JVM, and it fails all at once. A sort uses the disk gently: sorted runs the size of its buffer, merged F at a time, then one counting pass in order. A TreeMap holds the same keys, and threads share the same memory.

quiz.q: Two writers commit to the same Iceberg table on S3, both starting from `v7.metadata.json`. What makes sure exactly one of them becomes v8?
options: A compare-and-swap: a catalog's conditional update, or since 2024 an S3 write with `If-None-Match` or `If-Match`
S3's strong consistency alone
A lock on the table's folder
The last writer wins, and Iceberg merges the two later
quiz.why: A commit may swap the pointer only if it still names the version the writer started from. Strong consistency makes reads current, but it doesn't stop two writers from both writing, and S3 has no folders to lock. Catalogs do the swap with a conditional update or an HTTP commit with requirements, and S3's conditional writes now offer the same building block.

quiz.q: A join stage has 200 tasks. 199 finish in 30 seconds, and one runs for 40 minutes after reading 30% of the shuffle data. What fixes it?
options: `spark.speculation=true`
More shuffle partitions
A bigger executor for every task
AQE's skew join (once its thresholds are met) or salting the hot key
quiz.why: One hot key lands in one partition however many partitions there are, and a speculative copy reads the same oversized partition. Splitting the key is the fix: AQE splits partitions over 5 times the median and 256 MB, or you salt the key and copy the matching rows of the other side.

quiz.q: In a star schema, shop 7 moves from LOW to HIGH risk. Which design keeps last quarter's report the same when it's run again?
options: Overwrite shop 7's dimension row (type 1)
Close shop 7's current version and add a new one with a new surrogate key (type 2), with each fact keeping the key valid on its day
Copy the risk level onto the fact rows, only for new payments
Delete shop 7's old payments
quiz.why: Type 2 keeps both versions, and each payment points at the version it was made under, so a rerun groups old payments by their old risk level. Type 1 moves the whole history into HIGH, and the other options lose or split data.

quiz.q: A merge-on-read Iceberg table takes a batch of corrections every 5 minutes. After a month, reads are slow and the storage has doubled, though the rows are right. What was missing?
options: Scheduled upkeep: compaction (`rewrite_data_files`), then `expire_snapshots`, and `remove_orphan_files` now and then
A bigger cluster
Switching to copy-on-write
A REST catalog instead of a JDBC one
quiz.why: Merge-on-read writes small data files and delete files that every reader must merge, and old snapshots keep old files alive. Compaction rewrites them into a few clean files, and expiry deletes the files only old snapshots used. Copy-on-write would rewrite large files every 5 minutes instead.

quiz.q: An Airflow task runs `INSERT INTO daily_totals SELECT ... WHERE day = '{{ ds }}'` with `retries=3`. Which change makes retries and backfills safe?
options: Lower `retries` to 1
Use `now()` instead of `ds`, so the data is always fresh
Run the backfill with `--max-active-runs 1`
Replace the day in one step (delete the day and insert it inside one transaction, or overwrite the partition)
quiz.why: An attempt that dies after its insert was saved leaves its rows, and the retry adds them again. Replacing the day makes a second run leave what the first did. Fewer retries make the double count rarer, not gone; `now()` breaks backfills; and backfill runs one at a time still double each day.

quiz.q: A fraud model's training data joins each payment to the card's newest feature row. On old payments it catches 98% of fraud; live, it catches 62%. What's the fix?
options: Train a more complex model
Join each payment to the newest row whose event time and write time are both at or before the payment (point in time)
Use only the oldest feature row of each card
Add more months of data
quiz.why: The newest rows were worked out after the payments, and they counted chargebacks caused by the very frauds being labelled: label leakage. A point-in-time join shows the model only what existed at the moment of the decision, which is what it sees live.

quiz.q: A nightly job works out new risk scores for 1 million shops, and the program that approves payments at the till reads them. How should the job publish them?
options: Build the new scores as a new version offline, check it, then switch a pointer to it in one step
UPDATE each shop's row in the live database as the job works it out
Empty the table, then insert the new scores
Email the file to the people who run the approving program
quiz.why: Row-by-row updates cost a round trip each, compete with live payments, show readers a mix of two runs, and leave half a table if the job dies; emptying the table leaves it blank for a while. A new version plus one pointer switch is all or nothing, and rollback is switching back.

quiz.q: On a laptop, the same filter, join and totals over 10 million payments take about 0.1 s in DuckDB and about 1.4 s in Spark's local mode. Why?
options: Spark reads Parquet row by row
DuckDB saves the answer and hands it out again
Spark pays for planning stages, scheduling tasks, writing and fetching shuffle files and running in the JVM, which only pay off across many machines
DuckDB skips the join
quiz.why: Both engines read by column and really run the join. Spark's fixed costs exist so that work can spread over machines and survive failures; on one machine they're pure overhead. The crossover comes when the data or the working set outgrows one machine.
